What a release means here, and what it deliberately leaves alone.

The releasable unit is the package, not the repository. `packages/lattice` is what a consumer installs from npm; `packages/lattice-vscode` is what a marketplace would serve. The root manifest is `private: true` and has no version anyone can depend on. So the entries below are package paths — release-please bumps each manifest, writes each changelog, and tags from the commits that touched that path.

`separate-pull-requests` is stated because with two packages its default flips. release-please defaults it to `packages.length === 1` (measured in release-please 17.11.1, manifest.js): with only the plugin listed it was implicitly true, and adding the second entry would silently switch to one merged pull request titled from `group-pull-request-title-pattern` — whose default, `chore: release main`, carries neither a version nor a per-package title. Separate pull requests keep the branch names, tags and titles each component already has, and let one component release without holding the other.

Each `pull-request-title-pattern` overrides a default that this repository would reject. release-please titles a release pull request `chore${scope}: release${component} ${version}`, where `${scope}` is the target branch — `chore(main): release 0.1.0`. CI runs commitlint on every pull request title (the squash subject is the one commit message the `commit-msg` hook never sees), and `main` is not in `commitlint.config.mjs`'s `scope-enum`: the release pull request would fail a required check and could never merge. The plugin keeps `workspace` — cutting the repository's principal release is an act of the repository. The extension uses `vscode`, its own entry in that enum, so the two release pull requests are distinguishable at a glance and both merge. Fixing it here rather than by adding `main` to the enum keeps the enum meaning what it says it means: one entry per package, plus the three that name a change owning no package.

`component` for the extension is stated because the default is wrong twice over: release-please derives it from the package's manifest `name`, which is `lattice` (the marketplace listing name), so the tag would read `lattice-v0.1.0` — indistinguishable from a tag for the repository itself. `lattice-vscode` names the directory, and `include-component-in-tag` (default true, deliberately not overridden the way the plugin's entry overrides it) keeps its tags `lattice-vscode-v*`, disjoint from the plugin's bare `v*`.

The workflow reading these outputs keys them by PATH, not component — `packages/lattice-vscode--release_created` — see the comment in .github/workflows/release.yml, which is the other half of this file.

No `extra-files` entry for `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, and that is not an oversight. That version keys Claude Code's plugin cache and moves when the manifest moves; this one is the tool's own and is what the language server announces as `serverInfo`. Tying them would force a plugin-cache bump on every release of code the manifest does not contain, and `src/conformance/plugin-catalogue.integration.test.mjs` already holds the manifest version to the marketplace entry that must match it. Two facts wearing one word.

`last-release-sha` is the M0 rename's clean slate: the plugin's manifest version drops to `0.0.0` at `packages/lattice` (renamed from `packages/nx-polyglot-graph`), so release-please's own history walk has to stop at the commit the rename landed on rather than searching further back for a release tagged under the old path, which it would not find (measured against release-please 17.11.1, `manifest.js`: the top-level `lastReleaseSha`, not `bootstrap-sha`, which is ignored once a release pull request has ever been generated — this repository's first one already had been). The pinned SHA is `2f4950e1f87f35c4834b6c42a57f7ea489bda6b6`, the commit `packages/nx-polyglot-graph` was renamed from.
